WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: First observation of gravitational waves
======================================================================

{{Short description|2015 detection made by LIGO interferometers}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2019}}
{{Infobox astronomical event
|redshift={{val|0.093|0.030|0.036}}<ref name="Improved" />
|distance={{circa}} 1.4 billion [[Light-year|ly]]
|energy={{val|3.0|0.5|0.5}} {{solar mass|link=y}} × ''c''<sup>2</sup><ref name="Properties" />{{efn|1=''c''<sup>2</sup> {{solar mass}} is about {{convert|1.787e47|J|foe J erg cal BTU kWh|lk=on|disp=out|sigfig=2}}, or {{convert|1.787e47|J|tTNT|lk=on|disp=out|sigfig=2}}.}}
 |name=GW150914|event_type=[[Gravitational wave]]|discovery={{circa}} 1.4 billion years ago <br />
(detected 14 September 2015, 9:50:45 UTC)|detected_by=[[LIGO]]|duration={{circa}} 200 milliseconds|progenitor=2 [[black holes]]|constellation=[[Southern celestial hemisphere|Southern hemisphere]]}}
The first direct observation of [[gravitational wave]]s was made on 14 September 2015 and was announced by the [[LIGO]] and [[Virgo interferometer|Virgo]] collaborations on 11 February 2016.<ref name="PRL-20160211" /><ref name="Nature_11Feb16" /><ref name="NYT-20160216">{{cite news |author=The Editorial Board |title=The Chirp Heard Across the Universe |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/16/opinion/the-chirp-heard-across-the-universe.html |date=16 February 2016 |work=[[New York Times]] |access-date=16 February 2016}}</ref> Previously, gravitational waves had been inferred only indirectly, via their effect on the timing of [[pulsars]] in [[binary star]] systems. The [[waveform]], detected by both LIGO observatories,<ref name="BBC_11Feb16" /> matched the predictions of [[general relativity]]<ref name="Pretorius2005">{{cite journal |last1=Pretorius |first1=Frans |author-link=Frans Pretorius |year=2005 |title=Evolution of Binary Black-Hole Spacetimes |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=95 |issue=12 |article-number=121101 |arxiv=gr-qc/0507014 |bibcode=2005PhRvL..95l1101P |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.95.121101 |issn=0031-9007 |pmid=16197061 |s2cid=24225193}}</ref><ref name="CampanelliLousto2006">{{cite journal |last1=Campanelli |first1=M. |author-link=Manuela Campanelli (scientist) |last2=Lousto |first2=C. O. |author-link2=Carlos Lousto |last3=Marronetti |first3=P. |last4=Zlochower |first4=Y. |year=2006 |title=Accurate Evolutions of Orbiting Black-Hole Binaries without Excision |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=96 |issue=11 |article-number=111101 |arxiv=gr-qc/0511048 |bibcode=2006PhRvL..96k1101C |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.96.111101 |issn=0031-9007 |pmid=16605808 |s2cid=5954627}}</ref><ref name="BakerCentrella2006">{{cite journal |last1=Baker |first1=John G. |last2=Centrella |first2=Joan|author2-link= Joan Centrella |last3=Choi |first3=Dae-Il |last4=Koppitz |first4=Michael |last5=van Meter |first5=James |title=Gravitational-Wave Extraction from an Inspiraling Configuration of Merging Black Holes |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=96 |issue=11 |article-number=111102 |year=2006 |issn=0031-9007 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.96.111102 |pmid=16605809 |arxiv=gr-qc/0511103 |bibcode=2006PhRvL..96k1102B|s2cid=23409406 }}</ref> for a [[gravitational wave]] emanating from the [[inspiral|inward spiral]] and [[Stellar collision|merger]] of [[Binary black hole|two black holes]] (of 36 {{solar mass|link=y}} and 29 {{solar mass}}) and the subsequent [[Binary black hole#Ringdown|ringdown]]{{efn|1=The ringdown phase is the settling down of the merged black hole into a sphere.<ref>{{cite journal |title=The black-hole collision that reshaped physics |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |first=Davide |last=Castelvecchi |volume=531 |issue=7595 |date=23 March 2016 |doi=10.1038/531428a |bibcode=2016Natur.531..428C |pages=428–431 |pmid=27008950|doi-access=free }}</ref>}} of a single, 62 {{solar mass}} black hole remnant. The signal was named '''GW150914''' (from ''gravitational wave'' and the date of observation 2015-09-14).<ref name="PRL-20160211" /><ref name="Naeye">{{cite news |last=Naeye |first=Robert |url=http://www.skyandtelescope.com/astronomy-news/gravitational-wave-detection-heralds-new-era-of-science-0211201644/ |title=Gravitational Wave Detection Heralds New Era of Science |work=Sky and Telescope |date=11 February 2016 |access-date=11 February 2016}}</ref> It was also the first observation of a binary black hole merger, demonstrating both the existence of binary [[stellar-mass black hole]] systems and the fact that such mergers could occur within the current [[age of the universe]].

This first direct observation was reported around the world as a remarkable accomplishment for many reasons. Efforts to directly prove the existence of such waves had been ongoing for over fifty years, and the waves are so minuscule that [[Albert Einstein]] himself doubted that they could ever be detected.<ref>{{Citation |last=Pais |first=Abraham |author-link=Abraham Pais |date=1982 |title=Subtle is the Lord: The science and the life of Albert Einstein |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-853907-0 |pages=278–281 |chapter=The New Dynamics, section 15d: Gravitational Waves |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/subtleislordscie00pais }}</ref><ref name ="renn">{{cite web |last1=Blum |first1=Alexander |last2=Lalli |first2=Roberto |last3=Renn |first3=Jürgen |author-link3=Jürgen Renn |title=The long road towards evidence |url=http://www.mpg.de/9966773/background |work=[[Max Planck Society]] |date=12 February 2016 |access-date=15 February 2016}}</ref> The waves given off by the cataclysmic merger of GW150914 reached Earth as a ripple in [[spacetime]] that changed the length of a 1,120&nbsp;km LIGO effective span by a thousandth of the width of a [[proton]],<ref name="Naeye" /> proportionally equivalent to changing the distance to [[Proxima Centauri|the nearest star outside the Solar System]] by one hair's width.<ref name="Guardian_11Feb16" />{{efn|1=Diameter of a proton ~ 1.68–1.74&nbsp;[[femtometer]] (1.68–1.74{{e|-15}} m); ratio of proton/1000/4000 m = ~4{{e|-22}}; width of a human hair ~ 0.02–0.04 [[Millimetre#Measurement|millimeter]] (0.02–0.04{{e|-3}} m); distance to [[Proxima Centauri]] ~ {{convert|4.423|ly|m}}; ratio of hair/distance to star = 5–10{{e|-22}}}} The energy released by the binary as it spiralled together and merged was immense, with the energy of {{val|3.0|0.5|0.5}} ''c''<sup>2</sup> {{solar mass}} ({{val|5.3|0.9|0.8}}{{e|47}} joules or {{val|5300|900|800}} [[Foe (unit)|foes]]) in total radiated as gravitational waves, reaching a peak emission rate in its final few milliseconds of about {{val|3.6|0.5|0.4}}{{e|49}} [[watt]]s – a level greater than the combined [[Power (physics)|power]] of all light radiated by all the stars in the [[observable universe]].<ref name="PRL-20160211"/><ref name="Nature_11Feb16"/><ref name = "CBS2016-02-11">{{cite web |url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/einstein-was-right-scientists-detect-gravitational-waves-in-breakthrough/ |title=Einstein was right: Scientists detect gravitational waves in breakthrough |last=Harwood |first=W. |date=11 February 2016 |work=[[CBS News]] |access-date=12 February 2016}}</ref><ref name="Drake">{{Cite web |title=Found! Gravitational Waves, or a Wrinkle in Spacetime |url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/2016/02/160211-gravitational-waves-found-spacetime-science/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160212083049/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/2016/02/160211-gravitational-waves-found-spacetime-science/ |archive-date=12 February 2016 |work=[[National Geographic News]] |access-date=12 February 2016 |last=Drake |first=Nadia |author-link=Nadia Drake |date=11 February 2016}}</ref>{{efn|1=Since gravitational waves hardly ever interact with matter, the effects of the gravitational waves on a human located only one [[astronomical unit|AU]] from the merger event would have been extremely minor and unnoticed.<ref name = "Ouellette2016">{{cite interview |url=https://gizmodo.com/your-questions-about-gravitational-waves-answered-1758269933 |title=Your Questions About Gravitational Waves, Answered |interviewer=[[Jennifer Ouellette]] |first=Amber |last=Stuver |date=12 February 2016 |website=[[Gizmodo]] |publisher=Gawker Media |access-date=24 February 2016|quote=... Now assume that we are 2 m (~6.5 ft) tall and floating outside the black holes at a distance equal to the Earth's distance to the Sun. I estimate that you would feel alternately squished and stretched by about 165 nm (your height changes by more than this through the course of the day due to your vertebrae compressing while you are upright)&nbsp;...}}</ref>}}

The observation confirmed the last remaining directly undetected prediction of [[general relativity]] and corroborated its predictions of space-time distortion in the context of large scale cosmic events (known as [[Tests of general relativity|strong field tests]]). It was heralded as inaugurating a new era of [[gravitational-wave astronomy]], which enables observations of violent astrophysical events that were not previously accessible and allows for the direct observation of the earliest [[chronology of the universe|history of the universe]].<ref name="PRL-20160211" /><ref name="tests" /><ref name="astrophysics" /><ref name="CNN-A">[https://edition.cnn.com/2016/02/12/opinions/gravity-wave-team-conversation/ CNN quoting Prof. Martin Hendry (University of Glasgow, LIGO)] – ''"Detecting gravitational waves will help us to probe the most extreme corners of the cosmos – the event horizon of a black hole, the innermost heart of a supernova, the internal structure of a neutron star: regions that are completely inaccessible to electromagnetic telescopes."''</ref><ref name="BBC-A">{{cite news |last=Ghosh |first=Pallab |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-35524440 |title=Einstein's gravitational waves 'seen' from black holes |work=BBC News |date=11 February 2016 |access-date=19 February 2016 |quote=With gravitational waves, we do expect eventually to see the Big Bang itself.}}</ref> On 15 June 2016, two more detections of gravitational waves, made in late 2015, were announced.<ref name="NYT-20160615">{{cite news |last=Overbye |first=Dennis |author-link=Dennis Overbye |title=Scientists Hear a Second Chirp From Colliding Black Holes |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/06/16/science/ligo-gravitational-waves-einstein.html |date=15 June 2016 |work=[[New York Times]] |access-date=15 June 2016}}</ref> [[List of gravitational wave observations|Eight more observations]] were made in 2017, including [[GW170817]], the first observed merger of binary [[neutron star]]s, which was also observed in [[electromagnetic radiation]].

==Gravitational waves==
{{Main|Gravitational wave}}
[[File:Warped Space and Time Around Colliding Black Holes (Courtesy Caltech-MIT-LIGO Laboratory, produced by SXS project).webm|thumb|Video simulation showing the warping of [[space-time]] and gravitational waves produced, during the final inspiral, merge, and ringdown of black hole binary system GW150914<ref name="SXSproject">{{cite web |url=http://www.black-holes.org/gw150914 |title=GW150914: LIGO Detects Gravitational Waves |website=Black-holes.org |access-date=16 February 2016}}</ref>]]

[[Albert Einstein]] predicted the existence of gravitational waves in 1916,<ref>{{cite journal |author=Einstein, A |title=Näherungsweise Integration der Feldgleichungen der Gravitation |date=June 1916 |url=http://einstein-annalen.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/related_texts/sitzungsberichte |journal=[[Prussian Academy of Sciences|Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften Berlin]] |volume=part 1 |pages=688–696|bibcode=1916SPAW.......688E }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Einstein, A |title=Über Gravitationswellen |date=1918 |url=http://einstein-annalen.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/related_texts/sitzungsberichte |journal=Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften Berlin |volume=part 1 |pages=154–167|bibcode=1918SPAW.......154E }}</ref> on the basis of his theory of [[general relativity]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Einstein |first=Albert |title=Die Grundlage der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie |date=1916 |journal=Annalen der Physik |volume=49 |issue=7 |pages=769–822 |url=http://www.alberteinstein.info/gallery/science.html |access-date=14 February 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060829045130/http://www.alberteinstein.info/gallery/gtext3.html |archive-date=29 August 2006 |bibcode=1916AnP...354..769E |doi=10.1002/andp.19163540702 |author-link=Albert Einstein}}</ref> General relativity interprets [[gravity]] as a consequence of distortions in [[spacetime]] caused by the presence of [[mass]], and further entails that [[Quadrupole formula|certain movements]] or acceleration of these masses will cause distortions – or "ripples" – in spacetime which spread outward from the source at the speed of light. Einstein considered this mostly a curiosity, since he understood that these ripples would be far too minuscule to detect using any technology foreseen at that time.<ref name ="renn"/> As a further consequence following from the [[conservation of energy]], the energy radiated away by gravitational waves from a system of two objects in mutual orbit would cause them to slowly spiral inwards, although again, this effect would be extremely minute and thus challenging to observe.<ref>
{{Cite book |author=Schutz, Bernard |title=A First Course in General Relativity |publisher=Cambridge University Press |edition=2 |date=31 May 2009 |isbn=978-0-521-88705-2 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/firstcourseingen00bern_0/page/234 234, 241] |chapter=9. Gravitational radiation |author-link=Bernard Schutz |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/firstcourseingen00bern_0 |url=https://archive.org/details/firstcourseingen00bern_0/page/234 }}
</ref>

One case where gravitational waves would be strongest is during the final moments of the merger of two [[compact star|compact objects]] such as [[neutron star]]s or [[black hole]]s. Over a span of millions of years, [[binary star|binary neutron stars]], and [[binary black hole]]s lose energy, largely through gravitational waves, and as a result, they [[Orbital decay#Gravitational radiation|spiral in]] towards each other. At the very end of this process, the two objects will reach extreme velocities, and in the final fraction of a second of their merger a substantial amount of their mass would theoretically be converted into gravitational energy, and travel outward as gravitational waves,<ref name="PhysicsWorld"/> allowing a greater than usual chance for detection. However, since little was known about the number of compact binaries in the universe and reaching that final stage can be very slow, there was little certainty as to how often such events might happen.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Predictions for the rates of compact binary coalescences observable by ground-based gravitational-wave detectors |journal=[[Classical and Quantum Gravity|Class. Quantum Grav.]] |author=LIGO Scientific Collaboration and VIRGO Collaboration |date=16 July 2010 |volume=27 |number=17 |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/27/17/173001 |arxiv=1003.2480 |bibcode=2010CQGra..27q3001A |article-number=173001|s2cid=15200690 }}</ref>

===Observation===
{{main|Gravitational-wave astronomy|List of gravitational wave observations}}
[[File:BBH gravitational lensing of gw150914.webm|thumb|Slow motion computer simulation of the black hole binary system GW150914 as seen by a nearby observer, during 0.33&nbsp;s of its final inspiral, merge, and ringdown. The star field behind the black holes is being heavily distorted and appears to rotate and move, due to extreme [[gravitational lensing]], as [[space-time]] itself is distorted and dragged around by the rotating black holes.<ref name="SXSproject" />]]

Gravitational waves can be detected indirectly – by observing celestial phenomena caused by gravitational waves – or more directly by means of instruments such as the Earth-based [[LIGO]] or the planned space-based [[Laser Interferometer Space Antenna|LISA]] instrument.<ref>{{cite web |date=8 August 2015 |title=Detecting Ripples in Space-Time, with a Little Help from Einstein |url=http://www.space.com/30203-observatory-to-spot-colliding-black-holes-in-space.html |first1=Kai |last1=Staats |first2=Marco |last2=Cavaglia |first3=Shivaraj |last3=Kandhasamy |website=[[Space.com]] |access-date=16 February 2016}}</ref>

====Indirect observation====
Evidence of gravitational waves was first deduced in 1974 through the motion of the double neutron star system [[PSR B1913+16]], in which one of the stars is a [[pulsar]] that emits electro-magnetic pulses at radio frequencies at precise, regular intervals as it rotates. [[Russell Alan Hulse|Russell Hulse]] and [[Joseph Hooton Taylor, Jr.|Joseph Taylor]], who discovered the stars, also showed that over time, the frequency of pulses shortened, and that the stars were gradually spiralling towards each other with an energy loss that agreed closely with the predicted energy that would be radiated by gravitational waves.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Weisberg |first1=J. M. |date=October 1981 |title=Gravitational waves from an orbiting pulsar |journal=Scientific American |volume=245 |issue=4 |pages=74–82 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican1081-74 |bibcode=1981SciAm.245d..74W |last2=Taylor |first2=J. H. |last3=Fowler |first3=L. A.}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Weisberg |first1=J. M. |date=2010 |title=Timing Measurements of the Relativistic Binary Pulsar PSR B1913+16 |journal=Astrophysical Journal |volume=722 |issue=2 |pages=1030–1034 |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/722/2/1030 |arxiv=1011.0718 |bibcode=2010ApJ...722.1030W |last3=Taylor |first3=J. H. |last2=Nice |first2=D. J.|s2cid=118573183 }}</ref> For this work, Hulse and Taylor were awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] in 1993.<ref>{{cite web |title=Press Release: The Nobel Prize in Physics 1993 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1993/press.html |publisher=Nobel Prize |access-date=6 May 2014 |date=13 October 1993}}</ref> Further observations of this pulsar and others in multiple systems (such as the [[double pulsar]] system [[PSR J0737-3039]]) also agree with general relativity to high precision.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Stairs |first=Ingrid H. |title=Testing General Relativity with Pulsar Timing |journal=Living Reviews in Relativity |date=2003 |volume=6 |issue=1 |article-number=5 |doi=10.12942/lrr-2003-5 |doi-access=free |pmid=28163640 |pmc=5253800 |arxiv=astro-ph/0307536 |bibcode=2003LRR.....6....5S}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Tests of general relativity from timing the double pulsar |last1=Kramer |first1=M. |display-authors=etal |arxiv=astro-ph/0609417 |journal=Science |volume=314 |issue=5796 |pages=97–102 |date=14 September 2006 |publication-date=6 October 2006 |doi=10.1126/science.1132305 |bibcode=2006Sci...314...97K |pmid=16973838|s2cid=6674714 }}</ref>

====Direct observation====
{{main|Gravitational-wave observatory|LIGO}}
[[File:Northern leg of LIGO interferometer on Hanford Reservation.JPG|thumb|Northern arm of the LIGO Hanford [[Gravitational-wave observatory]]]]
Direct observation of gravitational waves was not possible for many decades following their prediction, due to the minuscule effect that would need to be detected and separated from the background of vibrations present everywhere on Earth. A technique called [[interferometry]] was suggested in the 1960s and eventually technology developed sufficiently for this technique to become feasible.

In the present approach used by LIGO, a [[laser beam]] is split and the two halves are recombined after traveling different paths. Changes to the length of the paths or the time taken for the two split beams, caused by the effect of passing gravitational waves, to reach the point where they recombine are revealed as "[[Beat (acoustics)|beats]]". Such a technique is extremely sensitive to tiny changes in the distance or time taken to traverse the two paths. In theory, an interferometer with arms about 4&nbsp;km long would be capable of revealing the change of space-time – a tiny fraction of the size of a single [[proton]] – as a gravitational wave of sufficient strength passed through Earth from elsewhere. This effect would be perceptible only to other interferometers of a similar size, such as the [[Virgo interferometer|Virgo]], [[GEO 600]] and planned [[KAGRA]] and [[INDIGO]] detectors. In practice at least two interferometers would be needed because any gravitational wave would be detected at both of these, but other kinds of disturbances would generally not be present at both. This technique allows the sought-after signal to be distinguished from [[noise]]. This project was eventually founded in 1992 as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO). The original instruments were upgraded between 2010 and 2015 (to Advanced LIGO), giving an increase of around 10 times their original sensitivity.<ref>{{citation |title=LIGO Scientific Collaboration – FAQ; section: "Do we expect LIGO's advanced detectors to make a discovery, then?" and "What's so different about LIGO's advanced detectors?" |url=http://ligo.org/science/faq.php |access-date=16 February 2016}}</ref>

LIGO operates two [[Gravitational-wave observatory|gravitational-wave observatories]] in unison, located {{convert|3002|km|mi|abbr=on}} apart: the LIGO Livingston Observatory ({{Coord|30|33|46.42|N|90|46|27.27|W}}) in [[Livingston, Louisiana]], and the LIGO Hanford Observatory, on the [[Hanford Site|DOE Hanford Site]] ({{Coord|46|27|18.52|N|119|24|27.56|W|}}) near [[Richland, Washington]]. The tiny shifts in the length of their arms are continually compared and significant patterns which appear to arise synchronously are followed up to determine whether a gravitational wave may have been detected or if some other cause was responsible.

Initial LIGO operations between 2002 and 2010 did not detect any statistically significant events that could be confirmed as gravitational waves. This was followed by a multi-year shut-down while the detectors were replaced by much improved "Advanced LIGO" versions.<ref>{{cite web |title=Gravitational wave detection a step closer with Advanced LIGO |url=http://spie.org/newsroom/technical-articles/videos/ligo-hanford-spie-video |publisher=SPIE Newsroom |access-date=4 January 2016}}</ref>&nbsp;&nbsp;In February 2015, the two advanced detectors were brought into engineering mode, in which the instruments are operating fully for the purpose of testing and confirming they are functioning correctly before being used for research,<ref>{{cite web |title=LIGO Hanford's H1 Achieves Two-Hour Full Lock |url=https://www.advancedligo.mit.edu/feb_2015_news.html |date=February 2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150922064706/https://www.advancedligo.mit.edu/feb_2015_news.html |archive-date=22 September 2015 |access-date=11 February 2016 }}</ref> with formal science observations due to begin on 18 September 2015.<ref>{{cite journal |collaboration=LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration |last1=Abbott |first1=Benjamin P. |title=Prospects for Observing and Localizing Gravitational-Wave Transients with Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo |journal=Living Reviews in Relativity |year=2020 |volume=19 |issue=1 |page=3 |article-number=1 |doi=10.1007/lrr-2016-1 |pmid=28179853 |pmc=5256041 |arxiv=1304.0670 |bibcode=2016LRR....19....1A}}</ref>

Throughout the development and initial observations by LIGO, several "blind injections" of fake gravitational wave signals were introduced to test the ability of the researchers to identify such signals. To protect the efficacy of blind injections, only four LIGO scientists knew when such injections occurred, and that information was revealed only after a signal had been thoroughly analyzed by researchers.<ref name="firstperson" /> On 14 September 2015, while LIGO was running in engineering mode but without any blind data injections, the instrument reported a possible gravitational wave detection. The detected event was given the name GW150914.<ref name="Nature12Jan16" />

==GW150914 event==

===Event detection===
GW150914 was detected by the LIGO detectors in [[Hanford, Washington]], and [[Livingston, Louisiana]], at 9:50:45 [[UTC]] on 14 September 2015.<ref name="Nature_11Feb16" /><ref name="Naeye" /> The LIGO detectors were operating in "engineering mode", meaning that they were operating fully but had not yet begun a formal "research" phase (which was due to commence three days later on 18 September), so initially there was a question as to whether the signals had been real detections or simulated data for testing purposes before it was ascertained that they were not tests.<ref name="Nature16">{{cite journal |title=Gravitational waves: How LIGO forged the path to victory |journal=Nature |volume=530 |issue=7590 |pages=261–262 |first=Davide |last=Castelvecchi |doi=10.1038/530261a |date=16 February 2016 |publication-date=18 February 2016 |bibcode=2016Natur.530..261C |pmid=26887468|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The [[chirp|chirp signal]] lasted over 0.2 seconds, and increased in frequency and amplitude in about 8 cycles from 35&nbsp;Hz to 250&nbsp;Hz.<ref name="PRL-20160211" /> The signal is in the [[audible range]] and has been described as resembling the [[Bird vocalization|"chirp" of a bird]];<ref name="Nature_11Feb16"/> astrophysicists and other interested parties the world over excitedly responded by imitating the signal on [[social media]] upon the announcement of the discovery.<ref name="Nature_11Feb16"/><ref name="NYT-20160211-mr">{{Cite news |title=Scientists Chirp Excitedly for LIGO, Gravitational Waves and Einstein |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/12/science/scientists-chirp-excitedly-for-ligo-gravitational-waves-and-einstein.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=11 February 2016 |access-date=13 February 2016 |issn=0362-4331 |first=Michael |last=Roston}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.smh.com.au/technology/sci-tech/gravitational-waves-how-they-sound-and-why-scientists-are-going-nuts-20160211-gms4bc.html |title=Gravitational waves: how they sound and why scientists are going nuts |date=12 February 2016 |last=Strom |first=Marcus |newspaper=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Drake |first1=Nadia |title=Gravitational Waves Were the Worst-Kept Secret in Science |url=http://phenomena.nationalgeographic.com/2016/02/12/to-rumor-or-not-to-rumor-ligo-leaks-and-professional-responsibility/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160213093732/http://phenomena.nationalgeographic.com/2016/02/12/to-rumor-or-not-to-rumor-ligo-leaks-and-professional-responsibility/ |archive-date=13 February 2016 |work=National Geographic |date=12 February 2016}}</ref> (The frequency increases because each [[orbit]] is noticeably faster than the one before during the final moments before merging.)

The trigger that indicated a possible detection was reported within three minutes of acquisition of the signal, using rapid ('online') search methods that provide a quick, initial analysis of the data from the detectors.<ref name="PRL-20160211"/> After the initial automatic alert at 9:54 UTC, a sequence of internal emails confirmed that no scheduled or unscheduled injections had been made, and that the data looked clean.<ref name="firstperson">{{cite magazine |title=Here's the first person to spot those gravitational waves |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/here-s-first-person-spot-those-gravitational-waves |first=Adrian |last=Cho |date=11 February 2016 |magazine=[[Science (magazine)|Science]] |doi=10.1126/science.aaf4039}}</ref><ref name="newyorker">{{cite magazine |title=Gravitational Waves Exist: The Inside Story of How Scientists Finally Found Them |first=Nicola |last=Twilley |date=11 February 2016 |magazine=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref> After this, the rest of the collaborating team was quickly made aware of the tentative detection and its parameters.<ref name="mpg1">{{cite interview |title=The signal caught our eye immediately |url=http://www.mpg.de/9952303/gravitational-waves-interview |first1=Bruce |last1=Allen |subject-link1=Bruce Allen (physicist) |first2=Alessandra |last2=Buonanno |subject-link2=Alessandra Buonanno |first3=Karsten |last3=Danzmann |publisher=Max Planck Society |interviewer=Felicitas Mokler |access-date=11 February 2016 |date=11 February 2016}}</ref>

More detailed statistical analysis of the signal, and of 16 days of surrounding data from 12 September to 20 October 2015, identified GW150914 as a real event, with an estimated significance of at least [[Standard deviation|5.1 sigma]]<ref name="PRL-20160211"/> or a [[confidence level]] of 99.99994%.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.wired.com/2016/02/scientists-spot-the-gravity-waves-that-flex-the-universe/ |title=LIGO's First-Ever Detection of Gravitational Waves Opens a New Window on the Universe |author=Sarah Scoles |date=11 February 2016 |magazine=WIRED}}</ref> Corresponding wave peaks were seen at Livingston seven milliseconds before they arrived at Hanford. Gravitational waves propagate at the [[speed of light]], and the disparity is consistent with the light travel time between the two sites.<ref name="PRL-20160211"/> The waves had traveled at the speed of light for more than a billion years.<ref name="SA-20160212">{{Cite web |title=The Future of Gravitational Wave Astronomy |url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-future-of-gravitational-wave-astronomy/ |website=[[Scientific American]] |date=12 February 2016 |access-date=13 February 2016 |first=Lee |last=Billings}}</ref>

At the time of the event, the [[Virgo interferometer|Virgo gravitational wave detector]] (near Pisa, [[Italy]]) was offline and undergoing an upgrade; had it been online it would likely have been sensitive enough to also detect the signal, which would have greatly improved the positioning of the event.<ref name="Nature_11Feb16" /> [[GEO600]] (near [[Hannover]], Germany) was not sensitive enough to detect the signal.<ref name="PRL-20160211" /> Consequently, neither of those detectors was able to confirm the signal measured by the LIGO detectors.<ref name="Nature_11Feb16" />

===Astrophysical origin===
[[File:MergingBlackHoles V2.jpg|thumb|Simulation of merging black holes radiating gravitational waves]]
The event happened at a [[luminosity distance]] of {{val|440|160|180}} [[megaparsec]]s<ref name="Improved">{{Cite journal|arxiv=1606.01210 |title=An improved analysis of GW150914 using a fully spin-precessing waveform model |journal=Physical Review X |volume=6 |issue=4 |article-number=041014 |author=The LIGO Scientific Collaboration and The Virgo Collaboration |doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.6.041014 |year=2016 |bibcode=2016PhRvX...6d1014A |s2cid=18217435 }}</ref>{{Rp|6}} (determined by the amplitude of the signal),<ref name="Nature_11Feb16" /> or {{val|1.4|0.6}} billion [[light year]]s, corresponding to a cosmological [[redshift]] of {{val|0.093|0.030|0.036}} (90% [[credible interval]]s). Analysis of the signal along with the inferred redshift suggested that it was produced by the merger of two [[black hole]]s with masses of {{val|35|5|3}} times and {{val|30|3|4}} times the mass of the [[Sun]] (in the source frame), resulting in a post-merger black hole of {{val|62|4|3}} {{solar mass}}.<ref name="Improved"/>{{Rp|6}} The [[mass–energy equivalence|mass–energy]] of the missing {{val|3.0|0.5}} {{solar mass}} was radiated away in the form of gravitational waves.<ref name="PRL-20160211" />

During the final 20 milliseconds of the merger, the power of the radiated gravitational waves peaked at about {{Val|3.6|e=49|u=watts}} or 526 [[dBm]] – 50 times greater<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/science/science-news/12152347/Watch-live-Scientists-expected-to-announce-existence-of-Einsteins-gravitational-waves.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160212014009/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/science/science-news/12152347/Watch-live-Scientists-expected-to-announce-existence-of-Einsteins-gravitational-waves.html |archive-date=12 February 2016 |title=Moment scientists reveal major gravitational wave finding |date=11 February 2016 |first=Sarah |last=Knapton |newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]}}</ref> than the combined power of all light radiated by all the stars in the [[observable universe]].<ref name="PRL-20160211"/><ref name="Nature_11Feb16"/><ref name="CBS2016-02-11"/><ref name="Drake"/> The amount of this energy that was received by the entire planet Earth was about 36 billion joules, of which only a small amount was absorbed.<ref>[https://www.forbes.com/sites/startswithabang/2020/02/15/ask-ethan-could-gravitational-waves-ever-cause-damage-on-earth/ Could Gravitational Waves Ever Cause Damage On Earth?]</ref>

Across the 0.2-second duration of the detectable signal, the relative tangential (orbiting) velocity of the black holes increased from 30% to 60% of the [[speed of light]]. The orbital frequency of 75&nbsp;Hz (half the gravitational wave frequency) means that the objects were orbiting each other at a distance of only 350&nbsp;km by the time they merged. The [[phase (waves)|phase]] changes to the signal's [[polarization (waves)|polarization]] allowed calculation of the objects' orbital frequency, and taken together with the [[amplitude]] and pattern of the signal, allowed calculation of their masses and therefore their extreme final velocities and orbital separation (distance apart) when they merged. That information showed that the objects had to be black holes, as any other kind of known objects with these masses would have been physically larger and therefore merged before that point, or would not have reached such velocities in such a small orbit. The highest observed neutron star mass is 2 {{solar mass}}, with a conservative [[Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit|upper limit]] for the mass of a stable neutron star of 3 {{solar mass}}, so that a pair of neutron stars would not have had sufficient mass to account for the merger (unless exotic alternatives exist, for example, [[Exotic star#Boson stars|boson stars]]),<ref name="Properties" /><ref name="PRL-20160211" /> while a black hole-[[neutron star]] pair would have merged sooner, resulting in a final orbital frequency that was not so high.<ref name="PRL-20160211" />

The decay of the waveform after it peaked was consistent with the damped oscillations of a black hole as it relaxed to a final merged configuration.<ref name="PRL-20160211" /> Although the inspiral motion of compact binaries can be described well from [[Post-Newtonian expansion|post-Newtonian calculations]],<ref>{{cite journal |title=Gravitational Radiation from Post-Newtonian Sources and Inspiralling Compact Binaries |first=Luc |last=Blanchet |journal=[[Living Reviews in Relativity]] |doi=10.12942/lrr-2014-2 |pmid=28179846 |pmc=5256563 |arxiv=1310.1528 |year=2014 |volume=17 |issue=1 |article-number=2 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2014LRR....17....2B}}</ref> the strong gravitational field merger stage can only be solved in full generality by large-scale [[numerical relativity]] simulations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Campanelli |first1=Manuela |last2=Lousto |first2=Carlos |last3=Marronetti |first3=Pedro |last4=Zlochower |first4=Yosef |title=Accurate Evolutions of Orbiting Black-Hole Binaries without Excision |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.96.111101 |arxiv=gr-qc/0511048 |year=2006 |volume=96 |issue=11 |pmid=16605808 |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |article-number=111101 |bibcode=2006PhRvL..96k1101C|s2cid=5954627 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Post-Newtonian and numerical calculations of the gravitational self-force for circular orbits in the Schwarzschild geometry |first1=Luc |last1=Blanchet |first2=Steven |last2=Detweiler |first3=Alexandre |last3=Le Tiec |first4=Bernard F. |last4=Whiting |journal=[[Physical Review D]] |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.81.064004 |arxiv=0910.0207 |year=2010 |volume=81 |issue=6 |article-number=064004 |bibcode=2010PhRvD..81f4004B|s2cid=119163802 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Why Numerical Relativity? |url=http://www.black-holes.org/the-science-numerical-relativity/numerical-relativity/why-numerical-relativity |website=www.black-holes.org |publisher=SXS project |access-date=16 February 2016 |archive-date=27 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160327093233/http://www.black-holes.org/the-science-numerical-relativity/numerical-relativity/why-numerical-relativity }}</ref>

In the improved model and analysis, the post-merger object is found to be a [[rotating black hole|rotating Kerr black hole]] with a spin parameter of {{val|0.68|0.05|0.06}},<ref name="Improved" /> i.e. one with 2/3 of the [[Black hole#Physical properties|maximum possible angular momentum]] for its mass.

The two stars which formed the two black holes were likely formed about 2 billion years after the [[Big Bang]] with masses of between 40 and 100 times the mass of the [[Sun]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Belczynski |first1=Krzysztof |last2=Holz |first2=Daniel E. |last3=Bulik |first3=Tomasz |last4=O'Shaughnessy |first4=Richard |date=23 June 2016 |title=The first gravitational-wave source from the isolated evolution of two stars in the 40–100 solar mass range |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=534 |issue=7608 |pages=512–515 |doi=10.1038/nature18322 |issn=0028-0836 |pmid=27337338 |arxiv=1602.04531 |bibcode=2016Natur.534..512B|s2cid=1328036 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/2016/06/gravitational-waves-stars-ripples-space-time-origins-astronomy |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160622185632/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/2016/06/gravitational-waves-stars-ripples-space-time-origins-astronomy/ |archive-date=22 June 2016 |title=Ancient Stars Unleashed a Space-Time Tsunami Felt on Earth |date=22 June 2016 |website=news.nationalgeographic.com |access-date=22 June 2016}}</ref>

===Location in the sky===
Gravitational wave instruments are whole-sky monitors with little ability to resolve signals spatially. A network of such instruments is needed to locate the source in the sky through [[triangulation]]. With only the two LIGO instruments in observational mode, GW150914's source location could only be confined to an arc on the sky. This was done via analysis of the {{val|6.9|0.5|0.4}} ms time-delay, along with amplitude and phase consistency across both detectors. This analysis produced a credible region of 150 deg<sup>2</sup> with a probability of 50% or 610 deg<sup>2</sup> with a probability of 90% located mainly in the [[Southern Celestial Hemisphere]],<ref name="Properties" />{{rp|7}}{{rp|fig 4}} in the rough direction of (but much farther than) the [[Magellanic Clouds]].<ref name="Nature_11Feb16" /><ref name="Naeye" />

For [[88 modern constellations by area|comparison, the area of the constellation]] [[Orion (constellation)|Orion]] is 594 deg<sup>2</sup>.<ref name="RASCconstellations" />

===Coincident gamma-ray observation===
The [[Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope]] reported that its Gamma-Ray Burst Monitor (GBM) instrument detected a weak [[gamma-ray burst]] above 50 keV, starting 0.4 seconds after the LIGO event and with a positional uncertainty region overlapping that of the LIGO observation. The Fermi team calculated the odds of such an event being the result of a coincidence or noise at 0.22%.<ref name="fermi_arxiv">{{Cite journal|title=Fermi GBM Observations of LIGO Gravitational Wave event GW150914 |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=826 |issue=1 |pages=L6 |arxiv=1602.03920 |first1=V. |last1=Connaughton |first2=E. |last2=Burns |first3=A. |last3=Goldstein |first4=M. S. |last4=Briggs |first5=B.-B. |last5=Zhang |display-authors=etal |doi=10.3847/2041-8205/826/1/L6 |year=2016 |bibcode=2016ApJ...826L...6C |s2cid=41946613 |doi-access=free }}</ref> However a gamma ray burst would not have been expected, and observations from the [[INTEGRAL]] telescope's all-sky SPI-ACS instrument indicated that any energy emission in gamma-rays and hard X-rays from the event was less than one millionth of the energy emitted as gravitational waves, which "excludes the possibility that the event is associated with substantial gamma-ray radiation, directed towards the observer". If the signal observed by the Fermi GBM was genuinely astrophysical, INTEGRAL would have indicated a clear detection at a significance of 15 sigma above background radiation.<ref name="Integral">{{cite journal |title=''INTEGRAL'' upper limits on gamma-ray emission associated with the gravitational wave event GW150914 |journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal Letters]] |first1=V. |last1=Savchenko |first2=C. |last2=Ferrigno |first3=S. |last3=Mereghetti |first4=L. |last4=Natalucci |first5=A. |last5=Bazzano |display-authors=etal |volume=820 |issue=2 |pages=L36|date=April 2016 |doi=10.3847/2041-8205/820/2/L36 |bibcode=2016ApJ...820L..36S |arxiv=1602.04180|s2cid=3463753 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The [[AGILE (satellite)|AGILE]] space telescope also did not detect a gamma-ray counterpart of the event.<ref name="AGILE_4Apr16" />

A follow-up analysis by an independent group, released in June 2016, developed a different statistical approach to estimate the spectrum of the gamma-ray transient. It concluded that Fermi GBM's data did not show evidence of a gamma ray burst, and was either background radiation or an Earth albedo transient on a 1-second timescale.<ref name=siegel>{{cite news |author-link=Ethan Siegel |last=Siegel |first=Ethan |date=3 June 2016 |title=NASA's Big Mistake: LIGO's Merging Black Holes Were Invisible After All |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/startswithabang/2016/06/03/nasas-big-mistake-ligos-merging-black-holes-were-invisible-after-all/#12ddfea176e3 |newspaper=Forbes |access-date=9 June 2016}}</ref><ref name=greiner>{{cite journal |last1=Greiner |first1=J. |last2=Burgess |first2=J.M. |last3=Savchenko |first3=V. |last4=Yu |first4=H.-F. |journal=The Astrophysical Journal Letters |volume=827 |issue=2 |doi=10.3847/2041-8205/827/2/L38 |arxiv=1606.00314 |title=On the GBM event seen 0.4 sec after GW 150914 |date=1 June 2016 |page=L38 |bibcode=2016ApJ...827L..38G|s2cid=118576283 |doi-access=free }}</ref> A rebuttal of this follow-up analysis, however, pointed out that the independent group misrepresented the analysis of the original Fermi GBM Team paper and therefore misconstrued the results of the original analysis. The rebuttal reaffirmed that the false coincidence probability is calculated empirically and is not refuted by the independent analysis.<ref name="Connaughton2018">{{cite journal |title=On the Interpretation of the Fermi-GBM Transient Observed in Coincidence with LIGO Gravitational-wave Event GW150914 |journal=The Astrophysical Journal Letters |first1=V. |last1=Connaughton |first2=E. |last2=Burns |first3=A. |last3=Goldstein |first4=M. S. |last4=Briggs | display-authors=etal |volume=853 |issue=1 |pages=L9 |date=January 2018 |doi=10.3847/2041-8213/aaa4f2 |arxiv=1801.02305|bibcode=2018ApJ...853L...9C |s2cid=3513893 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Siegel2018">{{cite news |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/startswithabang/2018/02/02/black-hole-mergers-might-actually-make-gamma-ray-bursts-after-all/ |title=Black Hole Mergers Might Actually Make Gamma-Ray Bursts, After All |work=Forbes |author-link=Ethan Siegel |last=Siegel |first=Ethan |date=2 February 2018 |access-date=14 February 2018}}</ref>

Black hole mergers of the type thought to have produced the gravitational wave event are not expected to produce gamma-ray bursts, as stellar-mass black hole binaries are not expected to have large amounts of orbiting matter. [[Avi Loeb]] has theorised that if a massive star is rapidly rotating, the centrifugal force produced during its collapse will lead to the formation of a rotating bar that breaks into two dense clumps of matter with a dumbbell configuration that becomes a black hole binary, and at the end of the star's collapse it triggers a gamma-ray burst.<ref name="fermi_woo">{{cite news |last1=Woo |first1=Marcus |title=LIGO's black holes may have lived and died inside a huge star |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2077783-ligos-black-holes-may-have-lived-and-died-inside-a-huge-star/ |access-date=17 February 2016 |work=New Scientist |date=16 February 2016}}</ref><ref name="Loeb">{{cite journal |title=Electromagnetic Counterparts to Black Hole Mergers Detected by LIGO |journal=[[The Astrophysical Journal Letters]] |first=Abraham |last=Loeb |volume=819 |issue=2 |pages=L21 |date=March 2016 |doi=10.3847/2041-8205/819/2/L21 |bibcode=2016ApJ...819L..21L |arxiv=1602.04735|s2cid=119161672 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Loeb suggests that the 0.4 second delay is the time it took the gamma-ray burst to cross the star, relative to the gravitational waves.<ref name="Loeb"/><ref name="GRB on BBH">{{cite news |last=Gough |first=Evan |url=http://www.universetoday.com/127463/did-a-gamma-ray-burst-accompany-ligos-gravitational-wave-detection/ |title=Did a Gamma Ray Burst Accompany LIGO's Gravity Wave Detection? |work=Universe Today |date=18 February 2016 |access-date=19 February 2016}}</ref>

===Other follow-up observations===
The reconstructed source area was targeted by follow-up observations covering [[Radio astronomy|radio]], [[Visible light astronomy|optical]], [[Infrared astronomy|near infra-red]], [[X-ray astronomy|X-ray]], and [[Gamma-ray astronomy|gamma-ray]] wavelengths along with searches for coincident [[neutrino]]s.<ref name="Properties" /> However, because LIGO had not yet started its science run, notice to other telescopes was delayed.{{citation needed|date=February 2016}}

The [[ANTARES (telescope)|ANTARES]] telescope detected no neutrino candidates within ±500 seconds of GW150914. The [[IceCube Neutrino Observatory]] detected three neutrino candidates within ±500 seconds of GW150914. One event was found in the southern sky and two in the northern sky. This was consistent with the expectation of background detection levels. None of the candidates were compatible with the 90% confidence area of the merger event.<ref name="LIGO-P1500271">{{Cite journal |url=https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-P1500271/public/main |title=High-energy Neutrino follow-up search of Gravitational Wave Event GW150914 with ANTARES and IceCube |journal=Physical Review D |volume=93 |issue=12 |article-number=122010 |date=12 February 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160215165041/https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-P1500271/public/main |archive-date=15 February 2016 |bibcode=2016PhRvD..93l2010A |last1=Adrián-Martínez |first1=S. |display-authors=etal |collaboration=ANTARES Collaboration, IceCube Collaboration, LIGO Scientific Collaboration, Virgo Collaboration|arxiv=1602.05411 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.93.122010 |s2cid=119218254 }}</ref> Although no neutrinos were detected, the lack of such observations provided a limit on neutrino emission from this type of gravitational wave event.<ref name="LIGO-P1500271"/>

Observations by the [[Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Mission]] of nearby galaxies in the region of the detection, two days after the event, did not detect any new X-ray, optical or ultraviolet sources.<ref name="arXiv:1602.03868" />

===Announcement===
{{redirect|Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger|other events|List of gravitational wave observations}}
[[File:PhysRevLett.116.061102.pdf|thumb|GW150914 announcement paper<br> (''click to access full PDF'')]]
The announcement of the detection was made on 11 February 2016<ref name="Nature_11Feb16" /> at a news conference in Washington, D.C. by [[David Reitze]], the executive director of LIGO,<ref name="BBC_11Feb16" /> with a panel comprising [[Gabriela González]], [[Rainer Weiss]] and [[Kip Thorne]], of LIGO, and [[France A. Córdova]], the director of [[National Science Foundation|NSF]].<ref name="Nature_11Feb16" /> [[Barry Barish]] delivered the first presentation on this discovery to a scientific audience simultaneously with the public announcement.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Barish |first1=Barry |title=New results on the Search for Gravitational Waves, CERN Colloquium, 2/11/2016 |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/2131411 |access-date=18 March 2016}}</ref>

The initial announcement paper was published during the news conference in ''[[Physical Review Letters]]'',<ref name="PRL-20160211"/> with further papers either published shortly afterwards<ref name="astrophysics"/> or immediately available in [[preprint]] form.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.7935/K5MW2F23|year=2016|author1=LIGO Scientific Collaboration|title=Data release for event GW150914|type=Data Set|url=https://losc.ligo.org/events/GW150914/ |website=Gravitational Wave Open Science Center}}</ref>

===Awards and recognition===
In May 2016, the full collaboration, and in particular [[Ronald Drever]], [[Kip Thorne]], and [[Rainer Weiss]], received the [[Fundamental Physics Prize|Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]] for the observation of gravitational waves.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/04/science/ligo-gravitational-wave-breakthrough-prize-yuri-milner.html |title=LIGO Gravitational Wave Researchers to Divide $3 Million |first1=Dennis |last1=Overbye |date=3 May 2016 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=4 May 2016}}</ref> Drever, Thorne, Weiss, and the LIGO discovery team also received the [[Gruber Prize in Cosmology]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://gruber.yale.edu/prize/2016-gruber-cosmology-prize |title=2016 Gruber Cosmology Prize |website=[[Gruber Foundation]] |access-date=4 May 2016}}</ref> Drever, Thorne, and Weiss were also awarded the 2016 [[Shaw Prize]] in Astronomy<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.shawprize.org/en/shaw.php?tmp=3&twoid=102 |title=Shaw Laureates 2016 |work=The Shaw Prize Foundation |access-date=26 June 2016 |archive-date=5 April 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180405041431/http://www.shawprize.org/en/shaw.php?tmp=3&twoid=102 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.caltech.edu/news/2016-shaw-prize-awarded-ligo-founders-50845 |title=2016 Shaw Prize Awarded to LIGO Founders |website=[[Caltech]] News |first=Whitney |last=Clavin |date=1 June 2016}}</ref> and the 2016 [[Kavli Prize]] in Astrophysics.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2016-06/b-9sp060116.php |title=Nine scientific pioneers to receive the 2016 Kavli Prizes |date=2 June 2016 |website=[[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]] EurekAlert! |access-date=2 June 2016 }}{{Dead link|date=September 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Barish was awarded the 2016 [[Enrico Fermi Prize]] from the [[Italian Physical Society]] (Società Italiana di Fisica).<ref>{{cite web |title=2016 Enrico Fermi Prize |url=http://www.primapagina.sif.it/article/466/il-premio-fermi-2016-alle-onde-gravitazionali |website=[[Italian Physical Society|Società Italiana di Fisica]]}}</ref> In January 2017, LIGO spokesperson [[Gabriela González]] and the LIGO team were awarded the 2017 [[Bruno Rossi Prize]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://aas.org/posts/news/2017/01/aas-announces-recipients-2017-prizes-and-awards |title=AAS Announces Recipients of 2017 Prizes and Awards |date=9 January 2017 |website=[[American Astronomical Society]] |access-date=21 January 2017}}</ref>

The 2017 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] was awarded to Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne "for decisive contributions to the LIGO detector and the observation of gravitational waves".<ref>{{cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 2017 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2017/press.html |publisher=The Nobel Foundation |date=3 October 2017 |access-date=3 October 2017}}</ref>

==Implications==
The observation was heralded as inaugurating a revolutionary era of [[gravitational-wave astronomy]].<ref name="Black Holes, Cosmic Collisions and the Rippling of Spacetime">{{Cite web |url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/observations/black-holes-cosmic-collisions-and-the-rippling-of-spacetime/ |title=Black Holes, Cosmic Collisions and the Rippling of Spacetime |work=Scientific American |last=Mack |first=Katie |date=12 June 2017 |access-date=1 July 2017}}</ref> Prior to this detection, astrophysicists and cosmologists were only able to make observations based upon [[electromagnetic radiation]] (including visible light, X-rays, microwave, radio waves, gamma rays) and particle-like entities ([[cosmic ray]]s, [[stellar wind]]s, [[neutrino]]s, and so on). These have significant limitations – light and other radiation may not be emitted by many kinds of objects, and can also be obscured or hidden behind other objects. Objects such as galaxies and nebulae can also absorb, re-emit, or modify light generated within or behind them, and [[compact star]]s or [[exotic star]]s may contain material which is dark and radio silent, and as a result there is little evidence of their presence other than through their gravitational interactions.<ref>{{cite web |title=Gravitational wave astronomy |url=http://www.einstein-online.info/elementary/gravWav/gw_astronomy |website=[[Einstein Online]] |publisher=[[Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics]] |year=2016 |access-date=24 February 2016 |archive-date=9 December 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151209015846/http://www.einstein-online.info/elementary/gravWav/gw_astronomy }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Gravitational wave astronomy |first1=Jordan B. |last1=Camp |first2=Neil J. |last2=Cornish |s2cid=15478999 |journal=[[Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science]] |publication-date=December 2004 |volume=54 |pages=525–577 |doi=10.1146/annurev.nucl.54.070103.181251|doi-access=free |bibcode=2004ARNPS..54..525C|year=2004 }}</ref>

===Expectations for detection of future binary merger events===
On 15 June 2016, the [[LIGO]] group announced an observation of another gravitational wave signal, named [[GW151226]].<ref>{{Cite journal |collaboration=LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration |last=Abbott |first=B. P. |date=15 June 2016 |title=GW151226: Observation of Gravitational Waves from a 22-Solar-Mass Binary Black Hole Coalescence |journal=[[Physical Review Letters]] |volume=116 |issue=24 |article-number=241103 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.241103 |pmid=27367379 |arxiv=1606.04855 |bibcode=2016PhRvL.116x1103A|s2cid=118651851 }}</ref> The Advanced LIGO was predicted to detect five more black hole mergers like GW150914 in its next observing campaign from November 2016 until August 2017 (it turned out to be [[List of gravitational wave observations|seven]]), and then 40 binary star mergers each year, in addition to an unknown number of more exotic gravitational wave sources, some of which may not be anticipated by current theory.<ref name="Naeye" />

Planned upgrades are expected to double the [[signal-to-noise ratio]], expanding the volume of space in which events like GW150914 can be detected by a factor of ten. Additionally, Advanced Virgo, [[KAGRA]], and a possible third LIGO detector in India will extend the network and significantly improve the position reconstruction and parameter estimation of sources.<ref name="PRL-20160211" />

[[Laser Interferometer Space Antenna]] (LISA) is a proposed space based observation mission to detect gravitational waves. With the proposed sensitivity range of LISA, merging binaries like GW150914 would be detectable about 1000 years before they merge, providing for a class of previously unknown sources for this observatory if they exist within about 10 megaparsecs.<ref name="astrophysics" /> [[LISA Pathfinder]], LISA's technology development mission, was launched in December 2015 and it demonstrated that the LISA mission is feasible.<ref>{{cite web |title=LISA Pathfinder exceeds expectations |publisher=elisascience.org |url=https://www.elisascience.org/news/top-news/lisa-pathfinder-exceeds-expectations |date=7 June 2016 |access-date=7 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160803124722/https://www.elisascience.org/news/top-news/lisa-pathfinder-exceeds-expectations |archive-date=3 August 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref>

A 2016 model predicted LIGO would detect approximately 1000 black hole mergers per year when it reached full sensitivity following upgrades.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

===Lessons for stellar evolution and astrophysics===
The masses of the two pre-merger black holes provide information about [[stellar evolution]]. Both black holes were more massive than previously discovered [[stellar black hole|stellar-mass black holes]], which were inferred from [[X-ray binary]] observations. This implies that the [[stellar wind]]s from their progenitor stars must have been relatively weak, and therefore that the [[metallicity]] (mass fraction of chemical elements heavier than hydrogen and helium) must have been less than about half the solar value.<ref name="astrophysics">{{Cite journal |title=Astrophysical implications of the binary black-hole merger GW150914 |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |collaboration=LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration |last1=Abbott |first1=Benjamin P. |date=20 February 2016 |volume=818 |issue=2 |pages=L22 |doi=10.3847/2041-8205/818/2/L22 |arxiv=1602.03846 |bibcode=2016ApJ...818L..22A|s2cid=209315965 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The fact that the pre-merger black holes were present in a [[binary star]] system, as well as the fact that the system was compact enough to merge within the age of the universe, constrains either binary star evolution or [[Stellar dynamics|dynamical formation]] scenarios, depending on how the black hole binary was formed. A significant number of black holes must receive low [[Stellar black hole#Black hole kicks|natal kicks]] (the velocity a black hole gains at its formation in a [[core-collapse supernova]] event), otherwise the black hole forming in a binary star system would be ejected and an event like GW would be prevented.<ref name="astrophysics" /> The survival of such binaries, through common envelope phases of high rotation in massive progenitor stars, may be necessary for their survival.{{clarify|date=March 2016}} The majority of the latest black hole model predictions comply with these added constraints.{{citation needed|date=February 2016}}

The discovery of the GW merger event increases the lower limit on the rate of such events, and rules out certain theoretical models that predicted very low rates of less than 1&nbsp;Gpc<sup>−3</sup>yr<sup>−1</sup> (one event per cubic gigaparsec per year).<ref name="PRL-20160211" /><ref name="astrophysics" /> Analysis resulted in lowering the previous upper limit rate on events like GW150914 from ~140&nbsp;Gpc<sup>−3</sup>yr<sup>−1</sup> to {{val|17|39|13}}&nbsp;Gpc<sup>−3</sup>yr<sup>−1</sup>.<ref name="BlackHoleRate" />

===Impact on future cosmological observation===
Measurement of the waveform and amplitude of the gravitational waves from a black hole merger event makes accurate determination of its distance possible. The accumulation of black hole merger data from cosmologically distant events may help to create more precise models of the history of the expansion of the universe and the nature of the [[dark energy]] that influences it.<ref name = "O'Neill2016">{{cite web |url=http://news.discovery.com/space/weve-detected-gravitational-waves-so-what-160213.htm |title=We've Detected Gravitational Waves, So What? |last=O'Neill |first=Ian |date=13 February 2016 |website=News.Discovery.com |publisher=Discovery Communications, LLC |access-date=20 February 2016 |quote=We will be able to measure the rate the universe is expanding, or how much dark energy there is in the universe to extraordinary precision |archive-date=17 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160317184241/http://news.discovery.com/space/weve-detected-gravitational-waves-so-what-160213.htm }}</ref><ref name = "Cooper2016">{{cite web |url=http://physicsworld.com/cws/article/news/2016/jan/21/are-gravitational-waves-being-redshifted-away-by-the-cosmological-constant |title=Are gravitational waves being 'redshifted' away by the cosmological constant? |last=Cooper |first=Keith |date=21 February 2016 |website=PhysicsWorld.com |publisher=Institute of Physics |access-date=20 February 2016}}</ref>

The [[Recombination (cosmology)|earliest universe]] is opaque since the cosmos was so energetic then that most matter was ionized and photons were scattered by free electrons.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://map.gsfc.nasa.gov/universe/bb_tests_cmb.html |title=Tests of Big Bang: The CMB |publisher=NASA |date=5 December 2014 |access-date=24 February 2016}}</ref> However, this opacity would not affect gravitational waves from that time, so if they occurred at levels strong enough to be detected at this distance, it would allow a window to observe the cosmos beyond the current [[visible universe]]. Gravitational-wave astronomy therefore may some day allow direct observation of the earliest [[chronology of the universe|history of the universe]].<ref name="PRL-20160211" /><ref name="tests" /><ref name="astrophysics" /><ref name="CNN-A" /><ref name="BBC-A" />

===Tests of general relativity===
{{main|Tests of general relativity}}
The inferred fundamental properties, mass and spin, of the post-merger black hole were consistent with those of the two pre-merger black holes, following the predictions of general relativity.<ref name="Pretorius2005" /><ref name="CampanelliLousto2006" /><ref name="BakerCentrella2006" /> This is the first test of general relativity in the very [[Tests of general relativity#Strong field tests: Binary pulsars|strong-field regime]].<ref name="PRL-20160211" /><ref name="tests">{{cite journal|last1=Abbott|first1=Benjamin P.|year=2016|title=Tests of general relativity with GW150914|url=http://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/56932/|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=116|issue=221101|article-number=221101|arxiv=1602.03841|bibcode=2016PhRvL.116v1101A|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.221101|pmid=27314708|s2cid=217275338|collaboration=LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration}}<!--|access-date=3 June 2016--></ref> No evidence could be established against the predictions of general relativity.<ref name="tests" />

The opportunity was limited in this signal to investigate the more complex general relativity interactions, such as tails produced by interactions between the gravitational wave and curved space-time background. Although a moderately strong signal, it is much smaller than that produced by binary-pulsar systems. In the future stronger signals, in conjunction with more sensitive detectors, could be used to explore the intricate interactions of gravitational waves as well as to improve the constraints on deviations from general relativity.<ref name="tests" />

===Speed of gravitational waves and limit on possible mass of graviton===
The speed of gravitational waves ('''''v<sub>g</sub>''''') is predicted by general relativity to be the speed of light ('''''c''''').<ref>{{Cite journal | author = W. W. SALISBURY | title = Velocity of Gravitational Waves | journal = Nature | volume = 224 | pages = 782–783 | year = 1969 | issue = 5221 | doi = 10.1038/224782a0| bibcode = 1969Natur.224..782S | s2cid = 4259664 }}</ref> The extent of any deviation from this relationship can be parameterized in terms of the mass of the hypothetical [[graviton]]. The graviton is the name given to an [[elementary particle]] that would act as the [[force carrier]] for gravity, in [[quantum gravity|quantum theories about gravity]]. It is expected to be massless if, as it appears, gravitation has an infinite range. (This is because the more massive a [[gauge boson]] is, the shorter is the range of the associated force; as with the infinite range of [[electromagnetism]], which is due to the massless [[photon]], the infinite range of gravity implies that any associated force-carrying particle would also be massless.) If the graviton were not massless, gravitational waves would propagate below lightspeed, with lower frequencies ('''''ƒ''''') being slower than higher frequencies, leading to dispersion of the waves from the merger event.<ref name="tests" /> No such dispersion was observed.<ref name="tests" /><ref name="PhysicsWorld" /> The observations of the inspiral slightly improve (lower) the upper limit on the mass of the graviton from Solar System observations to {{val|2.1|e=-58|u=kg}}, corresponding to {{val|1.2|e=-22|u=[[Electronvolt|eV]]/''c''<sup>2</sup>}} or a [[Compton wavelength]] ('''''λ<sub>g</sub>''''') of greater than {{10^|13}} km, roughly 1 light-year.<ref name="PRL-20160211" /><ref name="tests" /> Using the lowest observed frequency of 35&nbsp;Hz, this translates to a lower limit on '''''v<sub>g</sub>''''' such that the upper limit on '''1-''v<sub>g</sub>'' /''c''''' is ~&nbsp;{{val|4|e=-19}}.{{efn|1=Based on <math>v_g^2/c^2 = 1-\tfrac{c^2}{\lambda_g^2 f^2}</math>, obtainable from the "Tests of general relativity ..." paper (p. 13, "Thus, we have...") and the [[Planck–Einstein relation]].<ref name="tests" />}}

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Future of an expanding universe
======================================================================

{{Short description|Aspect of physical cosmology}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2023}}
{{Cosmology|expansion}}

Current observations suggest that the [[Expansion of the universe|expansion]] of the [[universe]] will continue forever. The prevailing theory is that the universe will cool as it expands, eventually becoming too cold to sustain life. For this reason, this future scenario popularly called "[[Heat death of the universe|Heat Death]]" is also known as the "Big Chill" or "Big Freeze". Some of the other popular theories include the [[Big Rip]], the [[Big Crunch]], the [[Big Bounce]], and the [[Big Slurp]].<ref name="urlcds.cern.ch">{{Cite journal |last1=Adams |first1=Fred C. |last2=Laughlin |first2=Gregory |date=1997-04-01 |title=A dying universe: the long-term fate and evolutionof astrophysical objects |url=https://journals.aps.org/rmp/abstract/10.1103/RevModPhys.69.337 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |language=en |volume=69 |issue=2 |pages=337–372 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.69.337 |arxiv=astro-ph/9701131 |bibcode=1997RvMP...69..337A |issn=0034-6861 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210517014117/https://cds.cern.ch/record/318436/files/9701131.pdf |archive-date=17 May 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=What Is the Ultimate Fate of the Universe?|url=https://map.gsfc.nasa.gov/universe/uni_fate.html|access-date=19 February 2023|website=WMAP's Universe |publisher=[[NASA]] |date=2015-06-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gunn |first=Alastair |date=2025-06-08 |title=End of the Universe: 4 ways our cosmic apocalypse could unfold |url=https://www.sciencefocus.com/space/how-the-universe-will-end |access-date=2026-02-14 |website=BBC Science Focus Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

If [[dark energy]]—represented by the [[cosmological constant]], a ''constant'' energy density filling space homogeneously,<ref name="carroll">{{cite journal |author=Carroll |first=Sean M. |author-link=Sean M. Carroll |year=2001 |title=The cosmological constant |journal=Living Reviews in Relativity |volume=4 |issue=1 |article-number=1 |arxiv=astro-ph/0004075 |bibcode=2001LRR.....4....1C |doi=10.12942/lrr-2001-1 |doi-access=free |pmc=5256042 |pmid=28179856 }}</ref> or [[Scalar field theory|scalar fields]], such as [[quintessence (physics)|quintessence]] or [[moduli (physics)|moduli]], ''dynamic'' quantities whose energy density can vary in time and space—accelerates the expansion of the universe, then the space between clusters of [[galaxies]] will grow at an increasing rate. [[Redshift]] will stretch ancient ambient photons (including gamma rays) to undetectably long wavelengths and low energies.<ref name=lun /> [[Star]]s are expected to form normally for 10<sup>12</sup> to 10<sup>14</sup> (1–100&nbsp;trillion) years, but eventually the supply of gas needed for [[star formation]] will be exhausted. As existing stars run out of fuel and cease to shine, the universe will slowly and inexorably grow darker.<ref name=dying>{{cite journal | last1 = Adams | first1 = Fred C. | last2 = Laughlin | first2 = Gregory | year = 1997 | title = A dying universe: the long-term fate and evolution of astrophysical objects | journal = Reviews of Modern Physics | volume = 69 | issue = 2| pages = 337–372 | doi = 10.1103/RevModPhys.69.337 | bibcode=1997RvMP...69..337A | arxiv=astro-ph/9701131| s2cid = 12173790 }}</ref><ref name=dying-IIE>Adams & Laughlin (1997), §IIE.</ref> If [[proton decay]] is correct, which currently remains unproven and against the fundamental principles of particle physics, the [[compact star|stellar remnants]] left behind will disappear, leaving behind only [[black hole]]s, which themselves eventually disappear as they emit [[Hawking radiation]].<ref name=dying-IV>Adams & Laughlin (1997), §IV.</ref> Ultimately, if the universe reaches [[thermodynamic equilibrium]], a state in which the temperature approaches a uniform value, it is highly unlikely any further [[work (thermodynamics)|work]] will be possible, resulting in a final heat death of the universe.<ref name="dying-VID">Adams & Laughlin (1997), §VID.</ref>

== Cosmology ==

Infinite expansion does not constrain the [[Shape of the universe|overall spatial curvature of the universe]]. It can be open (with negative spatial curvature), flat, or closed (positive spatial curvature), although if it is closed, sufficient [[dark energy]] must be present to counteract the gravitational forces or else the universe will end in a [[Big Crunch]].<ref name="calibrating">{{Cite book |last=Levin |first=Frank S. |title=Calibrating the cosmos: how cosmology explains our big bang universe |date=2007 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0-387-30778-7 |series=Astronomers' universe |location=New York}}</ref>

Observations of the [[Cosmic microwave background]] by the [[Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe]] and the [[Planck (spacecraft)|Planck mission]] suggest that the universe is spatially flat and has a significant amount of [[dark energy]].<ref name="wmap_5yr">{{Cite journal |last=Hinshaw |first=G. |author-mask=etal |date=2008 |title=Five-Year Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) Observations: Data Processing, Sky Maps, and Basic Results |url=https://lambda.gsfc.nasa.gov/product/map/dr3/pub_papers/fiveyear/basic_results/wmap5basic.pdf |journal=The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series |volume=180 |issue=2 |pages=225–245 |arxiv=0803.0732 |bibcode=2009ApJS..180..225H |doi=10.1088/0067-0049/180/2/225 |issn=0067-0049 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=planck2015XIII>{{Cite journal|title=Planck 2015 results. XIII. Cosmological parameters|date=1 September 2016|journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics|volume=594|pages=A13|doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201525830|bibcode=2016A&A...594A..13P|doi-access=free|author1=Planck Collaboration|last2=Ade|first2=P. A. R.|last3=Aghanim|first3=N.|last4=Arnaud|first4=M.|last5=Ashdown|first5=M.|last6=Aumont|first6=J.|last7=Baccigalupi|first7=C.|last8=Banday|first8=A. J.|last9=Barreiro|first9=R. B.|last10=Bartlett|first10=J. G.|last11=Bartolo|first11=N.|last12=Battaner|first12=E.|last13=Battye|first13=R.|last14=Benabed|first14=K.|last15=Benoît|first15=A.|last16=Benoit-Lévy|first16=A.|last17=Bernard|first17=J. -P.|last18=Bersanelli|first18=M.|last19=Bielewicz|first19=P.|last20=Bock|first20=J. J.|last21=Bonaldi|first21=A.|last22=Bonavera|first22=L.|last23=Bond|first23=J. R.|last24=Borrill|first24=J.|last25=Bouchet|first25=F. R.|last26=Boulanger|first26=F.|last27=Bucher|first27=M.|last28=Burigana|first28=C.|last29=Butler|first29=R. C.|last30=Calabrese|first30=E.|arxiv=1502.01589|display-authors=1}}</ref> In this case, the universe might continue to expand at an accelerating rate. The acceleration of the universe's expansion has also been confirmed by observations of distant [[supernovae]].<ref name="calibrating" /> If, as in the [[Lambda-CDM model|concordance model]] of [[physical cosmology]] (Lambda-cold dark matter or ΛCDM), dark energy is in the form of a [[cosmological constant]], the expansion will eventually become exponential, with the size of the universe doubling at a constant rate.{{citation needed|date=June 2025}}

If the theory of [[Inflation (cosmology)|inflation]] is correct, the universe went through an episode dominated by a different form of dark energy in the first moments of the Big Bang; but inflation ended, indicating an equation of state much more complicated than those assumed so far for present-day dark energy. It is possible that the dark energy equation of state could change again resulting in an event that would have consequences which are extremely difficult to parametrize or predict.{{Citation needed|date=June 2011}}

== Future history ==
In the 1970s, the future of an expanding universe was studied by the astrophysicist [[Jamal Nazrul Islam|Jamal Islam]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Islam |first=Jamal N. |date=March 1977 |title=Possible Ultimate Fate of the Universe |journal=Quarterly Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society |volume=18 |page=3 |bibcode=1977QJRAS..18....3I}}</ref> and the physicist [[Freeman Dyson]].<ref name=twoe>{{cite journal | last1 = Dyson | first1 = Freeman J. | year = 1979 | title = Time without end: Physics and biology in an open universe | journal = Reviews of Modern Physics | volume = 51 | issue = 3| pages = 447–460 | doi = 10.1103/RevModPhys.51.447 | bibcode=1979RvMP...51..447D}}</ref> Then, in their 1999 book ''[[The Five Ages of the Universe]]'', the astrophysicists [[Fred Adams]] and [[Gregory P. Laughlin|Gregory Laughlin]] divided the past and future history of an expanding universe into five eras. The first, the ''Primordial Era'', is the time in the past just after the [[Big Bang]] when [[star]]s had not yet formed. The second, the ''Stelliferous Era'', includes the present day and all of the stars and [[galaxies]] now seen. It is the time during which stars form from [[Molecular cloud|collapsing clouds of gas]]. In the subsequent ''Degenerate Era'', the stars will have burnt out, leaving all stellar-mass objects as [[compact star|stellar remnants]]—[[white dwarf]]s, [[neutron stars]], and [[black hole]]s. In the ''Black Hole Era'', white dwarfs, neutron stars, and other smaller [[astronomical objects]] have been destroyed by [[proton decay]], leaving only black holes. Finally, in the ''Dark Era'', even black holes have disappeared, leaving only a dilute gas of [[photons]] and [[leptons]].<ref name=fiveages />

This future history and the timeline below assume the continued expansion of the universe. If space in the universe begins to contract, subsequent events in the timeline may not occur because the [[Big Crunch]], the collapse of the universe into a hot, dense state similar to that after the Big Bang, will prevail.<ref name=fiveages /><ref name="dying-VA">Adams & Laughlin (1997), §VA.</ref>
